cards.headline: Israeli forces displace Palestinian families in Hebron military raids

pages.text: Israeli forces forcibly displaced Palestinian families from their homes in Hebron in the southern West Bank on November 5, 2026, following a previous 11-day military operation in the city. This occurred after Israeli troops had declared their withdrawal from Hebron on November 2, 2026. The Palestinian Wafa news agency reported that soldiers raided the Abu Sneineh neighborhood in the south of the city and stormed a six-story residential building, forcing residents to leave and converting the structure into a military outpost. Resident Kefah Abu Sneineh stated the building houses approximately 50 people, including women, children, patients, and elderly people, who were left without shelter.

In the Jaber neighborhood of Hebron, Israeli troops forcibly evicted Majed Jaber and his family of 10 from their home during a raid, converting the property into a military barracks, according to the Wafa news agency. These incidents followed an 11-day military siege during which more than 4,000 people were displaced from their homes. Many residents reportedly returned to find their homes damaged or demolished. Israeli forces have been active in Hebron since an October 23 attack in which two soldiers were shot and killed. The raids took place days after October 31, 2026, when thousands of Israeli settlers were expected to arrive in the city for the Jewish religious celebration of Chayei Sarah, also known as “The life of Sarah,” which commemorates the death of Abraham’s wife.

cards.headline: Yemen’s UN-recognised government dismisses ministers and officers following Houthi advances

pages.text: The UN-recognised government of Yemen has reshuffled its political and military leadership in an effort to regain territory lost to Houthi forces in September and to end a four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city. The dismissals and appointments follow a failed counteroffensive launched on 5 October that aimed to liberate the entire country from Houthi control, resulting in fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. On 2 November 2026, Reuters reported that Houthi forces were approximately 37 miles (60km) from Aden, the nominal seat of the UN-recognised government. Despite the air superiority of the government's ally, Saudi Arabia, progress has not been made on the ground, even as Saudi Arabia has had to defend against near-daily Houthi attacks on its military bases and airports.

The leadership shakeup reflects military setbacks and potential pressure to address the demands of southern Yemenis. The government relies on southern troops to resist Houthi advances, but these forces have stated they will only fight to defend land within the former South Yemen. Between 1967 and 1990, the country was divided into two separate entities. A movement centered around the banned Southern Transitional Council (STC) seeks to either return to that division or establish a more federated country. While the government has become dependent on these southern troops, not all southern separatists support the STC, an organization that overreached in January, which critics say allowed Saudi leadership to defer decisions regarding the southern question.

Political tensions persist regarding the role of Saudi Arabia and the STC. Claims have been made that STC leaders were coerced by the Saudis into dissolving the organization against their will. STC officials have increased their criticism of Saudi Arabia in the media, reflecting confidence that if the north is lost to the Houthis, the Saudis will be forced to allow the STC to operate openly. Additionally, critics have described the UN-backed government as a “hotel government,” noting that many senior figures are largely based in hotels in Riyadh rather than operating permanently from inside Yemen, and that the administration is dependent on Saudi money to pay salaries.

cards.headline: Belarus sentences Catholic priest to three years in prison

pages.text: Anatoly Parakhnevich, a 66-year-old Roman Catholic priest, has been sentenced to three years in prison in Belarus. The Viasna Human Rights Center, which designated Parakhnevich as a political prisoner, stated that the priest had openly opposed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, condemned Belarus’ role in the conflict, and organized aid collections for Ukrainians. Parakhnevich served as the parish priest for a Catholic parish in Alkovichy, located in the Vileika district of northwestern Belarus. He rejected the charges against him and intends to appeal the verdict.

A court in the Vileika district held a closed-door trial in October, resulting in Parakhnevich's conviction on charges of “extremism” and “insulting the authorities.” While the specific details of the case remain unknown, believers indicated that an initial charge of “treason” was replaced by these two charges. This sentencing follows a broader crackdown by Belarusian authorities on critical voices. President Alexander Lukashenko has governed the nation of 9.5 million people for more than three decades. His rule faced significant challenges following a 2020 presidential election that was widely seen as rigged, leading to street protests by tens of thousands of people and an ensuing crackdown that saw tens of thousands detained.

cards.headline: AI stocks plunge in US markets following midterm election results

pages.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks led a significant decline in United States markets following sweeping midterm election wins for Democrats. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 4.8 percent in midday trading, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 2.8 percent. The selloff was driven by losses in US chip and data centre-related stocks as investors weighed the impact of the election results on the AI industry. Data centre operators and neocloud companies experienced slumps, with Nebius Group down nearly 17 percent and CoreWeave down over 12 percent.

The market pressure follows the success of 39 ballot measures intended to restrict AI out of 45 total data centre ballot initiatives across the country. According to Data Centers on the Ballot, only one initiative in North Dakota voted against such restrictions. UBS analysts estimated to Reuters that potential construction pauses resulting from these measures could put roughly 30 percent of planned US data centre capacity additions in 2028 at risk. Analysts noted that concerns regarding these restrictions are reflected in the selloff across semiconductors and hyperscalers.

On November 11, 2026, US markets jumped following the midterm election, as Democrats' wins signaled limits on policy shocks from a Congress at odds with the White House. Markets were also reassured by remarks from US President Donald Trump stating he would accept the election results.

cards.headline: Melania Trump urges Russian and Ukrainian officials to choose 'humanity over war'

pages.text: Melania Trump brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House to urge both sides to choose “humanity over war” ahead of scheduled talks in Abu Dhabi. The event was staged to mark a six-day ceasefire that the First Lady helped broker in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky. The deal expired on November 1, 2026. Melania Trump said she was “involved in every stage of the planning” of the temporary ceasefire, which included reviewing aerial images and assessing hospital access and roadways. During the event, she stated, “We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, attended the face-to-face meeting and thanked the First Lady for her “distinguished humanitarian role” in securing the truce. Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump. Ukrainian representatives at the event included lawmaker David Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's party, and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman. Arakhamia encouraged the Slovenian-born First Lady to continue her peace efforts, telling her she did an “amazing job.”

The White House event precedes a planned trilateral meeting with officials from the US, Ukraine, and Russia scheduled for November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi. President Donald Trump, who did not attend the White House event, previously told reporters in October that his wife “does better than our professionals” regarding the Oleshky ceasefire. Separately, President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that a “very big” agreement to end the war in Ukraine is in the works, suggesting the deal might involve “all of Europe.” US envoy Jared Kushner also stated that the US, NATO, and European partners have held discussions aimed at addressing the security concerns of all sides to reduce the risk of future conflict.

cards.headline: Israeli President undecided on prime minister candidate despite Eisenkot securing majority endorsements

pages.text: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it remains unclear which candidate can break the political deadlock following a contested election, despite Gadi Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing endorsements from 67 of the 120 elected lawmakers in the Knesset. While Eisenkot is the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, Herzog stated that mutual vetoes between and within political blocs make it difficult to determine who has the best chance of forming a government. The president is scheduled to decide on November 8, 2026, which man should first attempt to build a coalition. In Israel’s political system, the largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial opportunity to build a stable ruling coalition.

The election results left both major contenders without a clear pathway to power. Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while the Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot holds 48 seats. Of the lawmakers consulted, 46 endorsed Netanyahu, and United Torah Judaism, which is often aligned with Netanyahu, did not endorse either man. Herzog indicated he would hold personal talks with some party leaders over the Israeli weekend and noted that while consultation results may appear clear, the political landscape remains complicated by internal disagreements.

Parties representing Israeli Palestinians, who constitute approximately 20% of the population, have emerged as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. This follows a shift in the political landscape where turnout among Arab Israelis more than doubled to about 80%. According to Haaretz, both Arab-majority parties reported backing Eisenkot. These groups include the Joint List, which holds 11 seats, and the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am, which holds eight seats.

cards.headline: Nigeria court rules nomination of Atiku Abubakar invalid and removes African Democratic Congress leadership

pages.text: A Federal High Court in Abuja, Nigeria, has removed the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) and ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid. The ruling comes approximately two months before presidential elections scheduled for 16 January, when Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi are expected to challenge President Bola Tinubu.

The legal dispute centered on the legitimacy of the ADC leadership. Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued that former Senate president David Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention. Gombe contended that he should have assumed leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025. David Mark currently serves as the party's interim chairman, a role assumed after several high-profile politicians, including Abubakar, joined the ADC in 2025 following factional infighting within the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

The ADC has challenged the ruling by Justice Peter Lifu, stating in a statement that the judgment was a calculated attempt to weaken the party and frustrate Abubakar's candidacy. The party described the decision as an attempt to stifle opposition momentum. Abubakar also raised legal concerns regarding the litigation, asking why a new case was filed to reopen the dispute after a previous ruling in July by judge Musa Liman had found that Mark was chosen in accordance with the party's constitution and national laws.

cards.headline: US Vice President JD Vance distances himself from President Trump's defense of Iran war following Republican midterm losses

pages.text: United States Vice President JD Vance has publicly broken from President Donald Trump's defense of the war with Iran following deep losses for the Republican Party in the midterm elections. Vance issued a lengthy social media post blaming the unpopular conflict for the GOP's defeat, questioning if the loss of the Senate for the next six years was worth the war. Vance, who has stated he will decide after the election whether to run for president in 2028, appears to be distancing himself from the president as he faces questions regarding his own political ambitions. In contrast, President Trump maintained his stance during an impromptu visit to a ballroom he is constructing at the White House, telling reporters, “The Iran thing, we had to do and we continue to do it.”

Reactions within Iran to the US election results vary among officials and commentators. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf argued that American voters delivered a verdict on the conflict, stating on X, “The Americans said no to war,” while also acknowledging that the rising cost of living contributed to the Republican losses. Ghalibaf mocked Vice President Vance's social media post, writing, “Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” Additionally, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, stated that Iran had dealt the United States a political setback in Washington after challenging the US on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz. The news website Etelaat Online suggested that the long-discussed “regime change” had occurred in the United States rather than in Iran.

Other Iranian leaders downplayed the impact of the midterm results on Washington's policy toward Tehran. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a statement saying that those who believe America can be persuaded to abandon its hostility toward Iran through partisan changes in the US political system are “gravely mistaken,” and he warned that Tehran would respond more forcefully to future US military action. Iran-based journalist and member of the reformist party Etemad-e Melli, Mohammad Sadegh Javadi Hesar, told DW that the election outcome was unlikely to affect Iran's calculations, noting that decisions regarding the conflict will ultimately be made in Washington. Tehran is expected to continue demanding an end to all hostilities, including in Lebanon, and the lifting of the US naval blockade.

cards.headline: Trump administration held secret talks with Iran regarding deportations, court documents show

pages.text: Unsealed court documents show the Trump administration held secret talks with Iranian officials to coordinate the deportation of Iranians, even as war continued in the region. The documents reveal that the administration maintained contact with Iran to submit travel documents and explore “possible avenues for removal.” An ongoing lawsuit alleges that U.S. immigration agencies shared confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, which the filings argue violates national immigration regulations and endangers individuals. The lawsuit describes a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody and pressure them to return to Iran, a move the filings state is a departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two nations.

As recently as mid-October, the Republican administration stated it had plans to deport Iranians through an unnamed third country, though the documents do not clarify when those deportations were intended to occur. During court proceedings, Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel stated that the government was “executing lawful orders of removal” after being questioned about sending individuals back to a region where they would face a “serious threat of certain death.” The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A judge in the case has ordered the government to provide the court with 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or any other country, as well as five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

cards.headline: Syria and Saudi Arabia sign defence cooperation and reconstruction deals

pages.text: Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman oversaw the signing of several agreements on November 4, 2026, including a defence cooperation deal and more than $403m in Saudi loans for Syria. The loans are intended for Syria’s energy, housing, health, and infrastructure sectors. This visit to Riyadh marks al-Sharaa’s second trip to the city in less than a month. While the Syrian Foreign Ministry described the cooperation agreement between the two countries’ defence ministries as the “most notable” of the deals, the ministry did not disclose the specific terms of the agreement.

The defence agreement follows statements regarding the Mecca alliance, a mutual defence pact involving Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan. On October 31, 2026, at the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said the Syrian government was evaluating whether to join the alliance. During the talks in Riyadh, al-Sharaa and Prince Mohammed discussed the regional and international situation, including the impact of military escalation on regional security, the safety of international shipping, the reliability of energy supplies, and global economic stability. Both leaders called for de-escalation and the peaceful resolution of disputes.

The ratification allows Ankara to provide military support to Riyadh as the kingdom faces attacks from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militants. cards.headline: British healthcare worker with Ebola being evacuated from DR Congo to UK

pages.text: A British healthcare worker has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and is being evacuated to the UK for medical treatment. The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition. According to an official document seen by Reuters, the individual is expected to arrive in the UK and then be transferred via specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit. A spokesperson for the UK government confirmed the case, stating that the UK has activated established procedures for such situations and that the risk to the UK public remains low. The worker was sent to the DRC by a humanitarian organisation to assist in responding to the current outbreak, which is the second largest on record. This is the first case in the current outbreak involving a British national.

The current Ebola outbreak in the DRC was declared on 15 May by the country's health ministry. Caused by the Bundibugyo virus, the outbreak has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths, making it the largest and deadliest in the country's history. It is the 17th Ebola outbreak identified in the DRC. Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with the blood, vomit, or other body fluids of infected people or dead bodies. While vaccine trials for the Bundibugyo virus are underway, there is currently no approved treatment. In the UK, high-level isolation units for infectious diseases are located at the Royal Free hospital in London, as well as in Newcastle and Liverpool.

cards.headline: China's carbon dioxide emissions fell 3.1% in third quarter, fastest rate since COVID-19 pandemic

pages.text: China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 3.1 percent between July and September, the fastest rate of decline since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to an analysis by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) published by Carbon Brief. The think tank attributed the drop to impacts from the war in the Middle East. As the world’s largest emitter, China is responsible for over 30 percent of global greenhouse gases. Severe disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has heavily impacted oil shipments to China, which is the world’s second-largest economy and the top importer of crude oil.

The CREA report, citing official figures and commercial data, stated that overall oil use fell by four percent year-on-year, while transport oil consumption decreased by nine percent. Coal use also fell by three percent year-on-year, despite the rapid construction of new coal plants in the country. CREA co-founder and lead analyst Lauri Myllyvirta told AFP that the shock has clearly accelerated the shift away from oil and the electrification trend, noting that China’s oil consumption had highly likely peaked before the shock. Myllyvirta added that a rebound in oil consumption may occur if or once prices come down.

Gao Yuhe, the Beijing-based project lead at Greenpeace East Asia, said that the downward trend in coal power is a key factor in the further development of renewable energy. While China has seen explosive growth in renewable installation and coal's share in its energy mix has edged down in recent years, Gao Yuhe noted the need for expanding the uptake of renewable energy, as well as the marketization of renewable energy and energy storage systems.

cards.headline: Canada's federal budget proposes C$142.1 billion in new spending to address sovereignty and homelessness

pages.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney has introduced a second federal budget, titled *Masters of Our Destiny*, which includes C$142.1 billion in new measures intended to build national sovereignty and address the high cost of living. The spending plan is supported by better-than-expected federal revenues from oil prices, which have been bolstered by the Iran War. Carney stated the budget is a step toward making the country more independent and less reliant on the United States for trade. Despite the new spending, the budget indicates that Carney has maintained his previous fiscal goals, even as the national deficit remains over C$50 billion ($36 billion; £27 billion) with no path to balance.

A central component of the budget is a plan to end homelessness in Canada within 10 years. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne described the initiative as one of the government's flagship policies. The budget proposes C$11.2 billion to tackle homelessness over four years and C$17.8 billion over 10 years. To achieve this, the federal government intends to create a new fund to support projects addressing health, addictions, and social supports. The strategy also includes a C$2 billion commitment to build new community mental health and addictions facilities, alongside continued support for the Veterans Homelessness Program.

The government's housing strategy aims to build 200,000 new homes across Canada over the next decade and expand non-market housing. Under the proposed plan, the federal government would cover capital costs for new supportive and transitional housing, while provincial and territorial governments would be responsible for ongoing operational costs, such as income, health, and training supports. The government intends to work toward signing agreements with provinces and territories before the spring economic update. This follows a 2025 federal count reporting approximately 65,000 people experiencing homelessness, while a 2022 Statistics Canada study found nearly one in eight households had experienced some form of homelessness, a rate that rises to more than one in four for Indigenous people.

cards.headline: Japan's nominal wages rise at fastest pace in almost 30 years

pages.text: Nominal wages in Japan rose 4.6% in September compared with a year earlier, marking the largest gain since 1997, according to a report from the labor ministry. This growth in pay suggests sustained momentum that may keep the Bank of Japan on track to hike interest rates as soon as December. Nominal wages represent the total amount of money workers receive before adjusting for inflation, whereas real cash earnings account for changes in purchasing power. Real cash earnings—adjusted for inflation excluding rents—climbed 2.2% from a year earlier, accelerating from a revised 1.6% gain in August and exceeding the consensus estimate of 1.3%. Economists had expected growth to slow due to fewer working days.

The labor ministry reported that base pay increased 3.7% in September. Additionally, a more stable gauge that excludes bonuses, overtime, and sampling distortions rose by a record 3.1% for full-time workers.

cards.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%

pages.text: The Bank of England has raised its base interest rate from 3.75% to 4%, marking the first increase in more than three years. The decision, which will affect mortgage borrowers, follows rising inflationary pressures linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The Bank's monetary policy committee (MPC) voted 8 to 1 for the increase, while the ninth member, Catherine Mann, favored a larger half-point increase instead.

The Bank expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of the year, an increase from the 3.2% projected in its July economic forecast. Inflation was measured at 3.5% in September via the consumer prices index. The Bank attributed these pressures to the Middle East conflict, which has kept oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel as hopes for a deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz have faded. Following the vote, the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall next, echoing forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility.

Bank governor Andrew Bailey signaled the possibility of another rate increase in the near future, noting that a resolution to the Iran conflict will be a key factor in future decisions. According to MPC minutes, Bailey stated that without news to soften inflationary risks, there is an argument for a further increase before taking a more conditional approach. However, he downplayed the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, despite market predictions.

cards.headline: Mexican judge accused of taking $2 million bribe to release suspected drug trafficker

pages.text: Luiz Benítez Alcántara, a 49-year-old Mexican judge, is accused by U.S. officials of accepting a $2 million bribe to release a suspected Canadian drug trafficker from custody. Benítez Alcántara was arrested in Colombia on November 1, 2026, and faces a nine-count U.S. grand jury indictment charging him with being an accessory after the fact. U.S. officials stated they will request his extradition from Colombia. Ciaran McEvoy, a spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles, said Benítez Alcántara was traveling to Colombia for personal reasons at the time of his arrest. It was not immediately known if he has a lawyer. If convicted, he could face a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison for each count, according to the Department of Justice.

The allegations involve the release of Andrew Clark, a 36-year-old Canadian citizen accused of playing a key role in a drug trafficking group allegedly headed by former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding. Benítez Alcántara was overseeing extradition proceedings in Mexico for Clark in 2024. Officials allege that between October 2024 and February 2025, Clark transferred approximately $2.75 million in small increments and through intermediaries in an attempt to be freed from Mexican custody. The indictment alleges Benítez Alcántara granted Clark bond and ordered his release in February 2025, the same day he allegedly received the $2 million bribe. Clark was arrested again days later and taken to the United States, where he faces drug trafficking and murder charges.

The case is part of a U.S. investigation into a multinational drug trafficking network allegedly run by Wedding, who was accused of moving cocaine from Latin America into the United States and orchestrating several killings. Wedding was arrested in Mexico and flown to California, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and drug charges. He remains in federal custody awaiting two trials. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche stated that public officials who assist drug traffickers will face justice in the United States. Bill Essayli, First Assistant U.S. Attorney in Los Angeles, told CBC News that authorities had long suspected Wedding was receiving help to evade capture, noting that multiple attempts to capture Wedding were undermined.

cards.headline: More than 600,000 people protest in France over cost of living and public services

pages.text: More than 600,000 protesters participated in rallies and marches across France during a day of action organized by five unions demanding increased wages and improved public services. While France's interior ministry reported the figure at more than 600,000, the left-wing CGT union estimated the number of participants at 1.57 million. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez noted that the total number of protesters grew throughout the afternoon, rising from 270,000 to 600,000 by the evening. The mobilization included workers from both the public and private sectors, as well as students. This wave of unrest began in September regarding poor resources and conditions at lycées (high schools) before expanding to universities, workers, and a revived movement against high prices known as the “yellow-vests.” Sophie Binet, head of the CGT union, stated the protests had reached a new level and that the mobilization would only halt if the government responded to their demands. Marylise Léon, leader of the CFDT union, previously stated she would be satisfied if the protests matched the scale of an earlier day of action on 17 October, when the interior ministry reported 550,000 participants and unions counted 800,000.

The demonstrations saw various reports of escalation and clashes despite being described as largely peaceful in some areas. In Lyon, hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing “black bloc” clashed with police, and a car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river. In the north-western city of Rennes, a local prefect reported that a “hostile group of masked individuals” gathered in front of the main union march, while authorities in the Brittany region said masked individuals attempted to block roads. In Bordeaux, a square was cleared using tear gas, and in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris, a teenager was injured in a stabbing involving a student during a high-school blockade. In central France, flames were reported rising from the roof of the Limoges town hall, and BFM TV reported a high school near Toulouse was set on fire. In Paris, police used tear gas and the Eiffel Tower remained closed for the day. To manage the unrest, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez deployed approximately 70,000 police officers and security forces, vowing an “extremely firm response” to potential violence. President Emmanuel Macron attributed the violence to ultra-left groups and promised additional security personnel at protests. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced he would convene a “social conference” with employers and unions.

cards.headline: Report: Calgary water system failures caused by decades of mismanagement and improper handling of previous reviews

pages.text: A provincial investigation has concluded that the failure of Calgary’s largest water main resulted from decades of mismanagement, underspending, and the “irregular and improper” handling of a 2015-16 water system review. The report, ordered by the Alberta government, suggests that addressing issues identified in that earlier review could have occurred long before the Bearspaw South feeder main (BPSFM) suffered catastrophic ruptures. The BPSFM carries approximately 60 per cent of Calgary’s fresh water and ruptured twice within an 18-month period, in June 2024 and December 2025. Former Alberta Energy Regulator chair David Goldie, who was enlisted by the province in March to conduct the deep dive, stated the failures were not simply about a pipe, but exposed weaknesses in how the city identifies infrastructure risks, assigns accountability, funds work, and reports risks to council.

Goldie’s team reviewed more than 58,000 documents and conducted 50 interviews with current and former city administrators, mayors, councillors, and staff to reach these conclusions. The investigation found that while reviews and analysis over two decades identified issues with the feeder main, the city did not properly inspect or repair those known problems. Furthermore, the report found that five out of nine recommendations from a 2015-16 external review by the utility advisory firm Raftelis never reached Calgary city council for consideration. While the Raftelis report did not find the water utilities were poorly run at that time, it highlighted structural weaknesses in governance and financial management that could undermine future decisions.

The report noted that from 2006 to 2024, Calgary spent roughly 35 per cent less than its approved capital budget, a figure that compared “unfavourably” with national benchmarks and did not keep pace with inflation or population growth. Goldie argued this indicated a problem with the city's planning and execution rather than a lack of funding, stating that the rates charged at the time would have funded the necessary work. The provincial report cost $1.2 million, a cost Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams described as being on par with similar inspections. In response to the findings, the city has already implemented several recommendations, including the creation of a new water oversight board and accelerating work to twin the Bearspaw feeder main. Goldie also recommended the city consider setting up an arms-length municipally-owned corporation (MCC) to oversee the utility, suggesting an independent assessment determine if such a corporation or Enmax is better suited for the role.

cards.headline: US midterm elections result in rejection of traditional Israel policy and Trump's Iran war

pages.text: The US midterm elections resulted in an unequivocal rejection of the traditional bipartisan consensus on Israel and Donald Trump's war in Iran. The results signal a shift in US politics following the war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians and has been widely described as a genocide. Even Donald Trump appeared to recognize the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability, suggesting on election morning that he would cut nearly $4bn in annual military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, in his words, “they don’t need it.” This suggestion was condemned by pro-Palestinian advocates as “desperate” and by pro-Israel advocates as “unserious.” Trump's proposal to replace military aid with arms sales suggested that while funding would continue, it would be harder to track.

cards.headline: UK government defends Supreme Court case to uphold Palestine Action terrorist designation

pages.text: A lawyer for the UK government defended the decision to ban Palestine Action as a “terrorist” organization before Britain’s highest court, arguing the group is not a “non-violent protest group.” The legal challenge follows a successful High Court appeal being overturned, leading co-founder Huda Ammori to take the case to the Supreme Court in London. The government's decision to proscribe the group in July 2025 places Palestine Action in the same category as organizations such as Al-Qaeda and Hezbollah, making it a criminal offense to publicly support the group. Those found guilty of belonging to or supporting Palestine Action could face up to 14 years in prison. The government maintains that no measure other than proscription could be “equivalently effective.”

The government's defense of the ban rests on the nature of the group's activities. James Eadie, a lawyer for the Home Office, told judges that Palestine Action's activities are “planned and undertaken secretly in order to avoid detection” and that the group is not part of a “long and honorable tradition of civil disobedience.” Eadie stated that “serious damage to property,” even without causing injury to people, could be considered “terrorism.” The proscription followed a series of protests targeting defense contractors and a UK military site that caused thousands of pounds worth of damage, including an incident where activists broke into a Royal Air Force base in southern England to spray-paint planes. Palestine Action describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime,” utilizing tactics such as graffiti, occupation, and lock-ons.

The legal battle has drawn significant opposition and support. Huda Ammori stated that the proscription has a disproportionate effect on freedom of speech and the right to protest, claiming the government is criminalizing legitimate protest as “terrorism” for the first time in British history. Ammori noted that Palestine Action has never advocated violence against any person. Conversely, two UK Jewish groups made legal submissions supporting the ban, stating the Jewish community is “especially vulnerable to Palestine Action’s violent activities.” Ammori’s lawyer, Raza Husain, rejected accusations of antisemitism, stating the group has never targeted Jewish people or businesses. cards.headline: Besieged Yemeni city of Taiz faces supply shortages and waste buildup as fighting escalates

pages.text: The besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is running out of basic goods and facing a buildup of uncollected waste as renewed fighting blocks supply lines and roads, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York that the collection of waste has ground to a halt because trucks are prevented from reaching dumping sites, increasing the risk of disease. In Taiz, sanitation workers report that snipers have been deployed near the main landfill site in the western part of the city, which is controlled by Iranian-backed Houthi forces. Workers have faced gunfire more than once while attempting to reach the site, and an acute shortage of fuel has further hampered collection efforts. Taiz generates between 550 and 600 tonnes of waste daily, or approximately 16,500 to 18,000 tonnes per month. As a result of the buildup, residents have resorted to burning rubbish in the streets, such as along the al-Saeed stream, exposing neighborhoods to toxic fumes and smoke.

The humanitarian situation in Yemen has been impacted by escalating hostilities. The UN reported that almost 310,000 people have been driven from their homes since the start of August. In Taiz, the prices of essential items have increased by as much as fivefold. Organizations delivering flour and other staple foods have pulled their trucks back to Al-Farsha, where they remain stranded. Separately, UNICEF, the UN Children’s Fund, reported an attack on the Al-Suqyah Health Center in Lahj Governorate that reportedly killed five people, including healthcare workers. The facility, which is supported by UNICEF, serves more than 1,700 people, including children.

The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, has registered nearly 5,400 newly displaced families for humanitarian financial assistance, with 4,200 of those families having received it so far. UNHCR has also provided shelter cash for more than 2,100 families in Aden, Abyan, and Lahj, and 3,000 relief kits are reportedly on their way to Aden. cards.headline: Developing countries' external debt reached a record $9.4 trillion in 2025

pages.text: External debt for low- and middle-income countries surged 5.5 per cent to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, according to the World Bank. This increase represents the largest annual jump since 2021, following the COVID pandemic. The Washington-based lender warned that the rise in debt threatens to crowd out essential investments in health, education, infrastructure, and jobs. World Bank chief statistician Haishan Fu stated that while the return of private lending to these countries is welcome, they are borrowing more and paying more, which in many cases leaves less for long-term development.

The World Bank's annual International Debt Report noted that borrowing from private creditors and bond issuance from public entities rose nearly 35 per cent to $251 billion, reaching its highest level in five years. External debt grew fastest among countries eligible for the International Development Association (IDA)—an institution that provides low- and zero-interest loans—with debt rising 8.1 per cent to $1.3 trillion in 2025. The lender noted that borrowing through international bond markets continued in 2026, raising questions regarding whether the terms are sustainable and if the capital reaches the people and places that need it most.

The poorest developing countries are facing high costs for new debt. These nations paid an average of 8.2 per cent on new private-creditor commitments, the highest rate since 1989, and 9.4 per cent on new bonds. In contrast, countries not eligible for IDA low- or zero-interest loans paid an average of 5.5 per cent on new bonds, a decrease from 5.8 per cent in 2024. Officials from the World Bank and other international financial institutions have recently expressed concern regarding high debt levels and the impact of higher interest rates on developing nations.

pages.text: American-made water pipes are being installed beneath Queen’s Park Crescent E. in Toronto, near the Ontario legislature, despite a trade war that has contributed to layoffs at Canadian steel companies. The city of Toronto awarded a $17.7-million contract to North York-based Gio Crete Construction Ltd. to replace water mains and resurface a section of road near downtown. To complete the work, Gio Crete Construction purchased pipes from an American steel water mains contractor in West Virginia. The city stated that using the American products was unavoidable in this instance, even as Canadian governments have attempted to use public buying power to prioritize local steel and automotive products in response to U.S. tariffs.

The use of American materials occurs amid a trade conflict in which President Donald Trump doubled tariffs on Canadian steel to 50 per cent. The economic impact of these tariffs has been felt by several Canadian steel producers. In March, hundreds of workers at Algoma Steel in Sault Ste. Marie were affected by layoffs. More recently, Stelco laid off more than 100 workers in Hamilton. Ron Wells, the president of United Steel Workers 1005 in Hamilton, said governments should go out of their way to ensure public money protects Canadian jobs during the trade war with the United States.

cards.headline: Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejects Toronto's bid for new funding agreement

pages.text: Ontario Premier Doug Ford has dismissed the prospect of negotiating a new funding agreement with the City of Toronto, stating that the province is facing “tough times” that will limit the provincial treasury. Ford told reporters, “There’s no [New Deal] 2.0,” and added that Toronto has to be “responsible for their own budget.” This rejection comes as Toronto faces a $1-billion shortfall heading into a winter budget and as large portions of a previous funding agreement are set to expire at the end of the year. The province is currently projecting a deficit of nearly $17 billion.

The proposed new deal would follow a 2023 agreement between Ford and Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow. In that previous deal, the province took control of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway, providing the city with billions in financial relief. While city budget chief Shelley Carroll previously described the 2023 arrangement as a “stop-gap approach” that should be followed by a “long-term solution,” Ford indicated he is not interested in a similar new formal agreement. Carroll noted that rather than seeking a “blank cheque” or a “big one-off,” Toronto is seeking access to long-term funding. In the past, the city's requests for new revenue tools, such as a municipal sales tax, have been rejected by the province.

Provincial ministers expressed similar stances to the premier. Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy told reporters at Queen’s Park that a new deal with Toronto was “not our plan,” while Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack said he was “not aware of any specific negotiations” with Chow. While rejecting a new formal deal, Ford signaled a willingness to discuss helping Chow deliver certain priorities, specifically mentioning public safety funding if it leads to an increased police presence on Toronto’s public transit. A statement from Chow's office did not directly address the rejection but noted that the mayor looks forward to meeting with the premier to discuss shared priorities including housing, transit, and public safety.

cards.headline: New bronze statue of Canadian flying ace William Barker unveiled in Toronto

pages.text: A new bronze statue of Lt.-Col. William Barker, a Canadian World War I flying ace, was unveiled at Scrivener Square Park on Yonge Street in Toronto. The ceremony, which began around 1:30 p.m., included martial music, several speeches, and a commemorative Lancaster airplane flyover to mark the debut of the monument. This unveiling is part of an effort to commemorate Barker, whose grandson, Ian Mackenzie, stated his memory was nearly lost to time. Mackenzie, who is in his 70s, noted that while Barker was once as famous as a rock star, fewer people know of him today.

According to the RCAF Foundation, Barker is Canada's most decorated military aviator and flew during World War I alongside fellow Victoria Cross recipient Billy Bishop. Beyond his military service, the Manitoba-born Barker served as the first leader of the Royal Canadian Airforce (RCAF), was the first president of the Toronto Maple Leafs, and co-established the first commercial airline operating out of the Toronto Island airport with Billy Bishop. Barker is already honored by several other memorials, including a plaque at the Mount Pleasant Cemetery mausoleum, a statue at Billy Bishop Airport, and a statue in Ottawa.

cards.headline: Sunni and Alawi residents in Talkalakh, Syria, rebuild ties following years of sectarian violence

pages.text: Sunni and Alawi residents in Talkalakh, the largest town in western Homs Governorate, are rebuilding social ties following years of sectarian violence, displacement, and looting under the Assad regime. Despite fears of conflict when the Assad regime fell on December 8, 2024, the town has experienced little violence over the past two years and serves as a counterexample to the dominant narrative of sectarian violence in postwar Syria, particularly within Homs Governorate. This fragile calm is being supported by local security reforms, community initiatives, economic ties, and civil society-supported dialogues aimed at restoring social cohesion and civil peace.

The history of violence in Talkalakh was deeply personal, as many crimes were committed by men who joined regime militias early in the war and targeted their own neighbors. Families in the town experienced widespread detentions, killings, mass displacement, and systematic looting. While these violations were not unique to Talkalakh, the close proximity of different sects—who largely fell on opposite sides of the Syrian revolution—heightened local tensions. Residents have since worked to rebuild historic relations and return to normal life in the restive border town, though coexistence remains threatened by unresolved grievances and demands for transitional justice.

cards.headline: Talensi youth petition President Mahama over Nalaamtaaba mining dispute

pages.text: Youths in Talensi, located in the Upper East Region of Ghana, have petitioned President John Dramani Mahama to intervene in a mining dispute involving Nalaamtaaba Enterprise. The petitioners are calling for the police to enforce a court order that would allow Nalaamtaaba to resume mining operations at Gbane. Lawyer and activist Martin Kpebu led the group in a march through Bolgatanga to the Upper East Regional Coordinating Council, which received the petition on the President's behalf. Kpebu stated that the group wants the police to effectively police the Nalaamtaaba concession so that the company's leaders and workers can continue lawful mining activities. The dispute involves Nalaamtaaba Enterprise, a locally owned firm, and Earl International Group (Ghana) Gold Limited, a Chinese-owned company. Earl International, which was formerly known as Shaanxi Mining (Ghana) Limited, alleges that Nalaamtaaba is mining illegally within its concession. Although the Bolgatanga High Court ordered police on February 10 to provide the managing director of Nalaamtaaba with protection and assistance at the site, and later refused a request by Earl International to overturn that order, Kpebu alleged that some individuals have blocked the enforcement of the order despite the Inspector General of Police (IGP) and his legal team giving the go-ahead for implementation.

Kpebu warned that the stoppage of mining activities is deepening hardship for families, noting that Nalaamtaaba provides direct and indirect work to more than 1,000 people in Talensi. He characterized the resulting unemployment as a national security threat.

cards.headline: Water rationing in Recife, Brazil, falls along racial lines

pages.text: In the Ibura de Baixo neighborhood of the South Zone region in Recife, Brazil, residents face severe water scarcity and poor water quality. Jeyne Araújo, a 27-year-old resident, reports that running water flows for only six hours a day, forcing her to stockpile water in buckets and drums starting at 4 a.m. to prepare for the taps running dry.

The tap water collected by Araújo is described as smelling strongly of chemicals and frothing into a thick, soapy white foam. Araújo told Mongabay that the water arrives so full of chlorine that it is too unpleasant to use for drinking or cooking immediately. This poor quality has impacted her family's health; her 9-year-old son, Wesley, suffered from constant vomiting and stomach pain for six months. Doctors at Recife’s Areias Hospital traced his intestinal infection to porridge prepared with tap water.

To protect her son, Araújo uses a portion of her monthly Bolsa Família—a government social welfare program benefit of 950 reais (approximately $180)—to purchase jugs of bottled water at 6 reais ($1.12) each. This additional expense further strains her budget.

cards.headline: NASA astronauts cast US election votes from the International Space Station

pages.text: NASA astronauts Anil Menon, Luke Delaney, and Jessica Watkins have cast their votes in the US election from the International Space Station using a secure electronic system. Menon announced the process via a post on X, including a 29-second video showing an “I voted” sticker and a tour of his private cabin, which he described as his “polling station.” The votes were sent to Harris County, Texas, where they were officially recorded. Harris County is the typical electoral destination for NASA astronauts because it houses the Johnson Space Center in Houston, the agency's primary center for managing human spaceflight missions. This practice of voting from orbit began in 1997 after the Texas legislature passed a law allowing astronauts to vote while in space. American astronaut David Wolf was the first to utilize this, casting a vote from the Russian space station Mir.

The voting procedure utilizes NASA's existing space communications and navigation programme infrastructure to transmit data between the station and Earth. To vote, astronauts request an absentee ballot using the “Federal Post Card Application,” a form also used by US military personnel serving away from home. Once the ballot is completed on board, it is transmitted via the “Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System” to a ground antenna at NASA’s White Sands facility in Las Cruces, New Mexico. The ballot is then transferred to Mission Control at the Johnson Space Center before being forwarded to the relevant county election official. NASA states the process is subject to strict security measures, including encryption, so that only the astronaut and the authorized election official can see the contents of the ballot.

The three astronauts who cast votes arrived at the station on different missions. Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins launched on 1 October as part of SpaceX’s “Crew-13” mission. Anil Menon arrived in mid-July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft. They are currently living with four other crew members: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonauts Anna Kikina, Pyotr Dubrov, and Sergei Teteriatnikov. Kutryk and Teteriatnikov are also part of the “Crew-13” mission, while Dubrov and Kikina arrived with Menon on the Soyuz.

cards.headline: Coordinated political campaign fuels land invasion in Brazilian Amazon territory home to uncontacted group

pages.text: Around 500 people recently invaded Indigenous land in the Brazilian Amazon, a territory inhabited by the Igarapé Ipiaçava, an uncontacted Indigenous group. A Mongabay investigation indicates the occupation was not a spontaneous land grab but was driven by a carefully coordinated political campaign. Politicians and their supporters used a questionable new state law to justify efforts to occupy the land and open up the territory.

The investigation analyzed hundreds of illegal land registrations within the Ituna/Itatá territory. While politicians and influential agribusiness figures frequently claim in speeches and on social media that land occupation is driven by struggling rural producers seeking small holdings, the data suggests otherwise. Of the registrations analyzed, 97% were registered as medium or large properties.

cards.headline: South West Water leakage failures putting customer supplies at risk

pages.text: Regulators have warned that repeated failures by South West Water to address leaks and repair burst pipes are increasing the risk that customers will lose water supplies. In a joint letter dated 26 October, Ofwat, the Environment Agency, and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs told the privatised company that its shortcomings are unacceptable given ongoing drought conditions. The company, which serves 1.8 million people across the south-west of England, has reportedly failed to meet targets for reducing leaks and repairing pipes for seven years. Regulators have given the company six weeks to produce an action plan.

The leakage from South West Water's infrastructure is 18.5% above forecast and has increased since the previous year. The company currently leaks 113.5m litres of water a day, an amount equivalent to 45 Olympic swimming pools. Regulators stated that this leakage is 5.7m litres a day higher than expected and poses a risk to the security of customer supplies. While South West Water has urged households in certain areas to reduce water usage to help secure supplies, the company does not acknowledge the contribution its own leakage scale makes to the risk of outages.

The warning comes as severe drought is declared in parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex, and West Sussex. In Exeter and mid and east Devon, the drought affects approximately 325,000 people and thousands of businesses, who face the risk of regular supply cut-offs over coming weeks and months. Such outages could lead to economic losses and school closures. Nationally, about 82% of England remains in drought, and the Met Office has stated that 120% of typical rainfall is required over seven months to fully end drought conditions.

cards.headline: Ancient proteins from 400,000-year-old teeth suggest Homo erectus interbred with Denisovans

pages.text: Researchers have extracted ancient proteins from the enamel of six teeth to reveal that Homo erectus likely exchanged genes with Denisovans in East Asia approximately 400,000 years ago. The study, published in Nature by Qiaomei Fu from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and colleagues, challenges older models of human evolution that viewed ancient relatives as isolated branches or evolutionary dead ends that left no descendants. Instead, the findings suggest a history of interbreeding between different hominin species. This genetic legacy may have been passed on to living populations in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and across Southeast Asia.

The research team recovered biological information from fossils that are considered too old for DNA analysis. To achieve this, they extracted proteins from teeth found at three Chinese sites: Zhoukoudian (the location of the early 20th-century “Peking Man” fossils), Hexian, and Sunjiadong. All of these specimens date to around 400,000 years ago. Homo erectus is recognized as the first hominin to leave Africa, having moved into Eurasia nearly two million years ago, and remains the most geographically widespread human ancestor on record.

cards.headline: Adult female Belding’s ground squirrels survive hibernation more effectively near female kin

pages.text: Adult female Belding’s ground squirrels are more likely to survive from year to year when living near more adult female kin, according to a study published November 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One. Jill Mateo and colleagues at the University of Chicago, USA, found that this survival boost from nearby family members does not apply to males or young females. Belding’s ground squirrels are hibernating rodents inhabiting the mountains of California, Nevada, and Oregon. While young males leave their homes to find new territories, females remain in communal family groups. Within these groups, female kin alert one another to danger and protect each other’s offspring from infanticide.

To identify factors affecting survival, researchers analyzed two decades of mark-recapture data. This method involves researchers tagging squirrels and checking the subsequent year to determine if they survived. The analysis examined the impact of age, sex, weight, number of offspring, the number of nearby family members, and certain hormones, while also accounting for annual snowfall. The findings showed that heavier individuals were more likely to survive hibernation. Additionally, females had higher survival rates than males, while juvenile males experienced the highest mortality. A shorter snowy season and larger body size were also noted to improve female survival rates.

cards.headline: Repurposed ancestral gene saved cod ancestors from extinction

pages.text: A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals that the ancestors of codfishes survived a potential extinction by repurposing an ancestral gene. This genetic adaptation allowed the order Gadiformes to develop the large populations that eventually shaped the North Atlantic. Researchers from the Institut de Ciències del Mar (ICM-CSIC) and the Institute of Biotechnology and Biomedicine of the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (IBB-UAB) in Spain, along with the University of Bergen (UoB) in Norway, discovered that these fish recruited mechanisms used by freshwater fishes to aid egg ovulation to compensate for lost genetic functions.

The survival of these lineages depended on egg buoyancy, which allows eggs to float in the water column so ocean currents can transport them across distances. In marine fish, eggs achieve this buoyancy by becoming engorged with more than 90% water during the final stages of development, making them less dense than seawater. Without this influx of water, the eggs would sink to nonsurvivable depths like stones. While codfishes and their relatives lost the specific genes essential for this buoyancy, they survived by adapting mechanisms typically used for egg ovulation in freshwater species.

cards.headline: Disrupted deep sleep brain waves linked to memory decline and tau protein accumulation

pages.text: Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining episodic memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Episodic memory is the ability to recall specific personal experiences, such as childhood milestones or recent events like where a car was parked. While some memory decline is a common part of aging, these changes can become more severe in individuals developing Alzheimer's disease. Scientists do not yet fully understand why the ability to retrieve the sights, sounds, and details of past experiences weakens as people grow older.

The study was conducted by neuroscientist Omer Sharon and colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker. Their findings offer clues regarding the biological processes occurring inside the aging brain.

cards.headline: Single psilocybin dose restores sensory filtering in female mice modeling schizophrenia

pages.text: A single dose of psilocybin has produced a lasting improvement in sensory filtering among female mice bred to model aspects of schizophrenia, according to research published in Neuropsychopharmacology. While the dose triggered heightened immediate behavioral reactions in the mice, the improvement in sensory filtering lasted for days. Sensory filtering is the brain's ability to process relevant information while ignoring irrelevant stimuli; schizophrenia is a psychiatric disorder often characterized by hallucinations, delusions, social withdrawal, and difficulty filtering sensory information. The findings suggest that the immediate psychedelic-like effects of psilocybin and its longer-term influence on brain function may operate through distinct biological pathways that vary by sex.

Psilocybin is the primary psychoactive compound found in magic mushrooms. Once consumed, the body converts it into psilocin, a molecule that alters perception, mood, and thought by primarily activating serotonin 2A receptors on the surface of brain cells. While psilocybin is undergoing wide testing in clinical trials for depression and anxiety, its effects on schizophrenia remain poorly understood. Because psilocybin can temporarily mimic psychosis-like changes in perception and brain network connectivity in healthy people, modern clinical trials routinely exclude individuals with a personal or family history of psychotic disorders.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of human studies found that psychedelic-induced psychosis is rare, occurring in approximately 0.002 percent of population studies, 0.2 percent in uncontrolled trials, and 0.6 percent in randomized controlled trials. The same analysis estimated a 3.8 percent rate of long-lasting psychotic symptoms among patients with schizophrenia, but that figure was derived from two small, uncontrolled LSD studies conducted more than fifty years ago that were judged to have a high risk of bias. This leaves open questions regarding how brains vulnerable to psychosis respond to psychedelics. Understanding this vulnerability requires looking beyond serotonin to glutamate, the brain's primary excitatory chemical messenger.

cards.headline: Alcohol use disorders lead mental health admissions at Ho Teaching Hospital in Ghana

pages.text: Alcohol use disorders were the primary cause of mental health admissions at the Ho Teaching Hospital (HTH) in the Volta Region of Ghana, according to a retrospective study. The research, titled “Burden of Mental Health Conditions at Ho Teaching Hospital in the Volta Region of Ghana: A Retrospective Analysis of Admitted Cases from 2021 to 2025,” identified alcohol use disorders as the most frequent condition, accounting for 257 cases (24.6 per cent) of mental health admissions analyzed. Schizophrenia followed with 213 cases (20.3 per cent), and bipolar affective disorder was the third most common at 174 cases (16.6 per cent). The study was conducted by Sorengmen Amos Ziema and colleagues from HTH to increase awareness and provide data for stakeholder decision-making regarding mental health concerns.

The study analyzed secondary data from the Lightwave Health Information Management System (LHIMS) for all inpatients admitted with mental health conditions (MHCs) between January 2021 and September 2025. During this period, 1,047 patients, representing 1.8 per cent of the 56,990 total inpatients seen at the hospital, were admitted with MHCs. Annual admissions included 192 in 2021, 236 in 2022, 226 in 2023, 208 in 2024, and 185 from January to September 2025. The research findings were presented by Mr. Ziema at the 7th African Epidemiology Society and 1st Ghana Epidemiology Society Conference in Accra.

The study found that mental health conditions affected more males than females, with 628 males (60.0 per cent) and 419 females (40.0 per cent) among the admitted patients. Most patients were in their productive years, with a mean age of 40 years and a median age of 37 years. Patients aged 20 to 49 years accounted for approximately two-thirds of all cases, specifically: 27.0 per cent were aged 30-39, 23.0 per cent were aged 20-29, and 15.3 per cent were aged 40-49. Regarding residency, 975 patients (93.1 per cent) lived in the Volta Region, while a few cases originated from the Oti, Eastern, and Greater Accra Regions. Additionally, 67.6 per cent of patients were insured under the National Health Insurance Scheme, while 32.4 per cent were not insured.

cards.headline: Newly described dinosaur species may be the first known dinosaur to eat mostly fruit

pages.text: Researchers have described a dinosaur species, *Infernogallus jamesi*, that may be the first known dinosaur to have eaten mostly fruit. According to a study published October 10 in the journal *Nature Communications*, the creature possessed a mouth and jaw adapted for chewing soft foods, similar to the way frugivorous parrots eat fruit on November 5, 2026. While scientists have previously proposed that some dinosaur groups ate fruit, study co-author Thomas Dudgeon, an evolutionary ecologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada, told Reuters that there was never evidence to support those claims until now. The discovery suggests that dinosaur diets during the Cretaceous period were more diverse than previously thought, moving beyond the well-known categories of carnivores like *Tyrannosaurus rex* or large herbivorous sauropods.

The *Infernogallus jamesi* lived approximately 67 million years ago in the same region and time as *T. rex*. The species name *jamesi* honors the grandfather of one of the study's co-authors. The genus name *Infernogallus* translates to “hell chicken,” a name chosen because of the animal's small size and because its fossils—which include a partial skeleton and a nearly complete skull—were discovered in the Hell Creek Formation. This fossil-rich area stretches across Wyoming, the Dakotas, and Montana. Weighing an estimated 25 pounds, the animal was about the size of a turkey and was one of the smallest caenagnathids, a group of feathered, two-legged dinosaurs with beaks.
